blocks.h2: Reasons to Get a Sewer Camera Inspection
blocks.intro: Arlington Heights homeowners usually call us for one of these:

tiles.body: A home from the 1950s or 1960s likely has a clay lateral. A camera look before closing tells you what you're buying.

tiles.h3: Your Basement Backed Up in a Storm
tiles.body: The camera shows whether your own line is blocked or damaged, or whether the sewer was simply overloaded.

tiles.h3: You Rod the Line Every Year
tiles.body: If you're paying for rodding on a schedule, it's worth knowing whether a repair would end the cycle.
Check the line and the cast iron under the floor before new flooring and drywall go in.

blocks.h2: What We Find in Arlington Heights Sewer Lines
blocks.intro: Most homes here were built between 1940 and 1989. That shapes what the camera shows.

items.body: The most common finding in postwar homes. Fine roots at a few joints can be managed with rodding. A mat of roots at every joint points to lining.

items.h3: Scale and Cracks in Cast Iron
items.body: Inside the house, old cast iron often shows heavy scale and, in some homes, a crack along the bottom of the pipe.
Shifting soil and roots can push clay sections out of line. Paper catches on the lip and causes repeat clogs.
Standing water in the pipe means a low spot. We measure where it is so it can be fixed without guesswork.
If you're adding a bathroom to a postwar basement, a camera look at the main line first tells you whether the old clay can take the extra flow.

blocks.h2: How a Camera Inspection Works With Us

steps.body: No digging, no opening walls. If there's no cleanout, we'll tell you the options.
We record the footage and use a locator to mark where problems sit, down to the depth.
We walk you through the video, explain what matters and what doesn't, and give you a copy.

blocks.h2: Sewer Camera Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: Should I get a sewer inspection before buying a home in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: Yes, especially for homes built before 1980.
items.answer: Yes. A standard home inspection doesn't look inside the sewer line. For a home built before 1980, a camera inspection is a small step that can reveal a repair worth negotiating before you close.

items.q: Will the camera inspection damage anything?
items.preview: No. It goes in through an existing cleanout.
items.answer: No. The camera enters through a cleanout, so there's no digging and no cutting. If the cleanout is buried or missing, we'll explain the options before going further.

items.q: Can the camera find exactly where the problem is?
items.preview: Yes. A locator marks the spot and the depth from the surface.
items.answer: Yes. The camera head carries a transmitter. We trace it from above and mark the location and depth, so any repair targets the right spot.

items.q: Do I get a copy of the video?
items.preview: Yes. You keep the footage for your records or your buyer.
items.answer: Yes. You get the recording so you can show it to a buyer, a seller or anyone else involved.

items.q: How long does a sewer camera inspection take?
items.preview: Usually about an hour for a typical home.
items.answer: Usually about an hour, including finding the cleanout, running the camera to the main and walking you through the footage.

items.q: How much does a sewer camera inspection cost in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: It depends on access and line length. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on how we get into the line and how long it is. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
